title: The visual arts
subtitle: Cubism, evocative, subject matter
summary: Name the great schools of art, judge a work with precise adjectives from exquisite to pedestrian, and borrow the language of painting to talk about writing.

lesson.heading: Changing tastes
lesson.text: Throughout the centuries, people have tended to be **suspicious of** the new **art movements** of their period. At the end of the 19th century, the public were shocked by the Impressionists; later, Cubist and Surrealist works puzzled them in the same way. Nowadays those same images are **perfectly acceptable** everywhere, from posters to advertising campaigns.

examples.text: The artist's work was **deemed** morally dangerous.
Critics said the paintings **consisted of nothing of significance**.
Perhaps today's new movements in art will meet with less hostility in future.

lesson.heading: Schools of art
rows: late 19th century; aimed to represent the effects of light on people or scenes
early 20th century; depicts people or objects as a set of geometric shapes
early 20th century; shows unusual or impossible things happening
mid 20th century; has its origins in optical illusions
lesson.note: A school of art is an art movement. An art school is the place where students go to study art - the two are not the same.

lesson.heading: Talking about artists and their work
lesson.text: The **subject matter** of a work is its content - what it is about. Someone who is **visually literate** is educated with regard to art. A **dauber** is someone who paints quickly and carelessly, so calling an artist a dauber is clearly disapproving. If you are **inured to** criticism, it no longer affects you at all - you have developed a hard skin.

examples.text: Finn enjoys painting but he's a **dauber**, not an artist.
The **subject matter** of the painting is a street market at dawn.
The sculptor is now **inured to** criticism.
Constant advertising has made us more **visually literate** than our grandparents.

lesson.heading: Words for commenting on art, and their opposites
rows: new in a special and interesting way
intended for educated, intelligent people (often disapproving)
demanding considerable effort to be understood
inspiring great admiration because it is brilliant in some way
interesting because it is strange or mysterious
not intended to be taken seriously, despite appearing serious

lesson.heading: Art and metaphor
lesson.text: Words connected with painting are regularly used to talk about literature. A writer **paints** a character **in a certain light**; minor figures may be **shadowy** or **sketchy**; the central characters are **depicted** or **portrayed** with great sensitivity; and the whole book **illuminates** a theme.

examples.text: The writer **paints** his hero **in a fascinating light**.
Minor characters are more **shadowy** or **sketchy**, but they are also **depicted** quite powerfully.
The heroine is particularly **colourful**, and we see how her character is **shaped** and **moulded** by events.
The **image** he creates to **illuminate** the evils of slavery will remain with me for ever.

lesson.note: To treat something in a black-and-white fashion is to present it as a simple choice between good and bad.

lesson.heading: Word formation from the art verbs

lesson.text: Highbrow and lowbrow are about the intended audience, not about quality - and both can sound disapproving.

exercises.prompt: Match each school of art with its description.

pairs.right: late 19th century; the effects of light on people and scenes
early 20th century; objects as sets of geometric shapes
early 20th century; unusual or impossible things happening
mid 20th century; based on optical illusions

exercises.prompt: The ___ matter of his early paintings was almost always the sea.
exercises.hint: (= the content of a work of art)
exercises.explanation: Subject matter is the content of a painting or other work of art.

exercises.prompt: Constant exposure to advertising has made young people far more visually ___ than their grandparents were.
exercises.explanation: Someone visually literate is educated with regard to art and images.

exercises.prompt: 'Finn enjoys painting but he's a dauber, not an artist.' What does the speaker think of Finn's work?
options: A low opinion - dauber suggests speed and lack of care.
A high opinion - dauber suggests bold use of colour.
A neutral opinion - dauber simply means a painter.
A high opinion - dauber suggests a professional.
exercises.explanation: A dauber is someone who paints quickly and carelessly; the word is disapproving.

exercises.prompt: 'Curious as it now seems, the artist's work was deemed morally dangerous.' Where would you expect to read this?
exercises.explanation: Deem is typical of more formal speech or writing; in conversation you would say considered or thought.

exercises.statement: If a sculptor is inured to criticism, it upsets them badly.
exercises.explanation: Wrong - inured to means not affected by it at all; the sculptor has developed a hard skin.

exercises.statement: Matilda studied at an art school, where she became interested in the Cubist school of art.
exercises.explanation: Correct - an art school is a place where students study art, while a school of art is an artistic movement.

exercises.prompt: I think that the artist's cartoons are usually rather ___ as they are intended to appeal to a mass audience.
exercises.explanation: Lowbrow work is aimed at a wide, non-specialist audience; highbrow is its opposite.

exercises.prompt: When an artist sent in an ordinary red brick to an exhibition, no one was sure whether it was ___ or intended as a serious statement.
exercises.explanation: Something tongue-in-cheek is not meant to be taken seriously, despite appearing serious.

exercises.prompt: Although the artist's early work is very sophisticated, some of his later pieces are surprisingly ___ in style.
exercises.explanation: Primitive is the opposite of sophisticated - it lacks advanced skill and understanding.

exercises.prompt: The design on that china plate is ___ - however did they manage to paint such fine detail?
exercises.explanation: Exquisite means having rare beauty or delicacy; its opposite is clumsy.

exercises.prompt: Although his photographs are quite ___, it is worth making the effort to understand them.
exercises.explanation: Challenging work demands considerable effort to be understood; its opposite is undemanding.

exercises.prompt: Does each word usually carry positive associations, usually negative ones, or either?
Match each verb with the noun formed from it.
Put this sentence of literary criticism in order.
exercises.answer: The writer paints his hero in a fascinating light
exercises.explanation: Painting words are regularly used as metaphors for writing.
